params.text:
Let the idea
choose its form.

slides.notes: A pause in the argument. A short statement lets the room absorb the idea. Animation is optional; this composition works as a still.

slides.name: 5 · A heading can sit beside the argument.

params.text: A heading can sit beside the argument.
Use the left side to name the question.
Use the right side to develop the answer.
Keep the sequence editable and reveal it when useful.

slides.notes: Keep the headings and supporting points editable. Choose Side heading for a single argument, or Columns for parallel ideas. These are examples, not limits on your content.

slides.name: 6 · Parallel ideas need equal space.

params.text: A clear subject tells the audience where to look.
A useful example gives the idea something concrete.
A deliberate pause gives people time to think.

slides.notes: Keep the headings and supporting points editable. Choose Side heading for a single argument, or Columns for parallel ideas. These are examples, not limits on your content.

slides.name: 7 · Section · Opening a session
slides.notes: SECTION — full red, nothing on it but the words. The loudest surface in the theme, so keep it for the two or three moments you want the room to look up. Subtitle is optional.

slides.name: 8 · Mark Martin

params.text: Advanced Information Presentation & Visualisation. Research interests in data literacy, computing education and how people read charts under time pressure.

slides.notes: INTRODUCTION — who is standing at the front. Title is the name, subtitle the role, body the paragraph. Use it once, on your first meeting with a cohort.

slides.name: 9 · The purpose of visualization is insight, not pictures.

params.text: The purpose of visualization is insight, not pictures.

slides.notes: QUOTE — body is the quotation, subtitle the attribution. Long quotations wrap and shrink; if it runs past three lines it has stopped being a quote slide and wants to be a content slide.

slides.name: 10 · Section · Explaining and organising

params.text: Content, journey, mind map, keywords, italics, cards

slides.notes: The six layouts that carry an argument. Each takes the same bullets array and arranges it differently — so you can change your mind about the shape without retyping the words.

slides.name: 11 · Content — the plain bullet slide

params.text: One point per line, in the bullets list.
A tab inside a line makes the part before it a lead-in, so a point can carry its own sub-clause.
Reveal them one at a time with Build on Next, or show them all at once.

slides.notes: CONTENT — the workhorse. This one has Build on Next set to DIM: points already made stay on screen at 38% so the argument so far is still readable, while the eye is told where you are now. Set it to Hide instead when an earlier point would give away the next one.

slides.name: 12 · Journey — a route with milestones

params.text: Reveal each milestone as you explain it
Foundations: why we visualise at all.
Colour, scale and the grammar of graphics.

slides.notes: JOURNEY — numbers each point as a milestone (01, 02, 03) along a route. Reach for it for a course outline, a project timeline, or a handover. Text before the tab is the milestone label, text after is the detail.

slides.name: 13 · Where visualisation sits

params.text: What the eye does before the brain catches up.
Turning a number into a position, length or hue.
Letting the reader ask the next question.

slides.notes: MIND MAP — arranges the points around the title in the centre rather than down the page. Use it when the points are siblings with no order; use Journey when the order is the point.

slides.name: 14 · Key fact — one number, set large

params.text: Key fact — one number, set large
SHARE OF THE WORLD’S DATA CREATED IN THE LAST TWO YEARS

The subtitle above the number is its label; the number itself is never a build step.
Three supporting lines is the limit — past that the number stops being the point.
Say the number, then stop talking.

slides.notes: KEY FACT — for the one figure you want quoted back at you. Reach for it when a chart would bury the finding in axes: a single number needs no scale, no legend and no explanation of what the bars mean.

slides.name: 15 · People & structure — who is who
slides.notes: PEOPLE & STRUCTURE — one person per line: name, role, and who they report to. Leave the third column off and they sit at the top. With no reporting lines at all it draws a flat team in one row, which is the right shape for a project group or a panel.

slides.name: 16 · Stat tiles — the numbers that matter

params.text: Stat tiles — the numbers that matter
Read the chart first — before they read the caption
Found the legend — on first look
Asked a follow-up — after a clear chart

slides.notes: STAT TILES — each line is label · value · note, and the value is set large. Three to six tiles; three is the sweet spot. Under Design, the Ring style fills a circle to the number’s share and the Bar style adds a KPI bar under it — both read the leading number in the value.

slides.name: 17 · Versus — two columns, row by row

params.text: Versus — two columns, row by row
One hue per series, twelve series
Two hues: the series that matters, and everything else
A legend the eye has to travel to

slides.notes: VERSUS — the subtitle names the two columns ("Before | After", "Myth | Fact"). Each row is left · right, or row label · left · right when the rows need naming, as here. Rows build on Next so the comparison is argued one line at a time.

slides.name: 18 · Funnel — stages that narrow

params.text: What happens to a chart between the analyst and the reader
if the title did its job

slides.notes: FUNNEL — stage · value · note. When the values are numbers the band widths follow them, so a cliff draws as a cliff. Without numbers the bands narrow evenly. Design → Direction flips it to a pyramid.

slides.name: 19 · Timeline — dated events on a rail

params.text: Timeline — dated events on a rail
Where the ideas in this module came from
The bar chart and the line chart, in one atlas
The rose diagram takes an argument to Parliament
Semiology of Graphics — the visual variables named

slides.notes: TIMELINE — date · event · detail, up to eight. Dates are labels, not parsed, so "Week 3" or "Term 2" work. Design → Shape switches to the vertical spine, which gives each event a full line of detail.

slides.name: 20 · Stat tiles · rings
slides.notes:
STATS · RING — the same layout, Design → Tile style → Ring. The arc fills to the number’s share of a hundred.

The inspector warns you when there is more than one of them, and it is right to: an arc is compared less accurately than a length, so four rings are four dials nobody can line up. One hero number in a ring is the fair use.

slides.name: 21 · Stat tiles · KPI bars

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Two of three targets met — enrolment is the one to talk about.

slides.notes: STATS · BAR — Design → Tile style → Bar. This is the variant to prefer when the numbers are being compared, because length on a common baseline is the channel the eye reads most accurately. The line underneath is the takeaway field.

slides.name: 22 · Funnel · pyramid
slides.notes:
FUNNEL · UP — Design → Direction → Pyramid. Same data, widest at the bottom, for when the story is the base rather than the loss.

The drop between two stages is printed for you either way — −60%, −74% — because that is the number a reader is working out in their head. And the inspector will point out that a Sankey answers the same question while also showing where the missing ones went.

slides.name: 23 · Timeline · down the page

params.text: Why we visualise at all, and what a channel is
The grammar of graphics, and where it misleads
Saying why a chart fails, in writing

slides.notes: TIMELINE · DOWN — Design → Shape → Down. A spine with a paragraph per event, for when the detail matters more than the span. Across is the default and suits six short entries; down suits three long ones.

slides.name: 24 · Cards · stacked, one at a time

params.text: Cards · stacked, one at a time
Something in the data does not fit the story.
Go back to how it was collected.
Pick the idiom that answers the question.
Write the finding as a sentence on the slide.

slides.notes: CARDS · STACK — Design → Card style → Stacked. Every card lands in the same place, the one being talked about in front and the ones already made peeking out behind. Four things get four moments instead of competing for one glance, and the pile shows the room how far through the set you are. Needs Build on Next, which is on here.

slides.name: 25 · Cards · rows, for cards that have something to say

params.text: Cards · rows, for cards that have something to say
Three cards across is fine for three words and cruel to a definition.
The column narrows until the label breaks up, and the set reads as one card with three columns.
Down the slide instead — full width each, and only as much height as the words need.

slides.notes: CARDS · ROWS — Design → Card style → Rows. The variant to choose the moment a card carries a sentence rather than a phrase. Grid is the default and suits short labels; this suits definitions.

slides.name: 26 · Keywords — term and definition

params.text: A particular way of encoding data visually.
The pixels that carry meaning rather than decoration.

slides.notes: KEYWORDS — the tab splits each line into a term and its definition, set as a two-column row. The vocabulary slide. Build on Next reveals a row at a time.

slides.name: 27 · Italics — a phrase and its gloss

params.text: Italics — a phrase and its gloss
Two things moving together need not be connected.
Anscombe’s whole point in four scatterplots.

slides.notes: ITALICS — the same term/definition split as Keywords, but the term is set in italic display type and given more room. Better for a handful of phrases you want to dwell on; Keywords is better for a list of six.

slides.name: 28 · Cards — parallel items, side by side

params.text: Cards — parallel items, side by side
Define the purpose and the audience before opening the data.
Clean, validate, and know what is missing.
Choose the idiom that fits the question.

slides.notes: CARDS — items that are peers, arranged in a row with the number on the side rather than across the top, so four fit without shrinking. The card count drives the column ladder automatically: two cards are wide, six are narrow. Also on dim build here.

slides.name: 29 · Cards · picture cards — a photograph over each

params.text: Cards · picture cards — a photograph over each
What the reader notices in the first second.
Axes, legend, units — where am I?
The one difference the chart exists to show.
The sentence they would repeat to a colleague.

slides.notes: CARDS — the same layout with Design → Cards layout set to Picture cards. Every card gets an image slot above its copy; the dashed box is the placeholder until you paste a URL or drop a file under that card in the inspector. Design → Picture shape switches between portrait crops and letterboxed plates.

slides.name: 30 · Journey · stepper — a process in one glance

params.text: Journey · stepper — a process in one glance
What does the reader need to decide?
The smallest table that answers it.
The chart family that fits the relationship.
The finding, written as a sentence.

slides.notes: JOURNEY — the third mode. Numbered discs on one horizontal rail with the copy beneath, for a process read left to right. Route keeps the sequence vertical; Handover is two or three big columns; Stepper is the infographic idiom for "first, then, then".

slides.name: 31 · Section · Data and evidence

params.text: A table, and all twenty chart idioms

slides.notes: Table and chart read the same pasted text, so a range from a spreadsheet becomes either without retyping.

slides.name: 32 · Table — when the numbers are the point

params.text: Table — when the numbers are the point

params.data:
Dataset	Mean x	Mean y	Correlation
I	9.00	7.50	0.816
II	9.00	7.50	0.816
III	9.00	7.50	0.816
IV	9.00	7.50	0.816

slides.notes: TABLE — paste a range straight from Excel or Sheets; tabs and pipes both work, first row is the header. Build on Next reveals a row at a time. Reach for a table when the reader needs the exact value, a chart when they need the shape.

slides.name: 33 · Code that writes itself

params.text:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("attendance.csv")
by_week = (
    df["week"]
      .value_counts()
      .sort_index()
)
print(by_week.head())

slides.notes: CODE — a viewer, not an IDE. Source types onto the wall when you Present, so the room watches the idea form without you sharing a desktop. Next skips to the finished snippet. Keep it short enough to read from the back; for a long demo, use a Video slide of your editor instead.

slides.name: 34 · Chart — bar, for comparing magnitudes

params.data:
Region	Leave %	Remain %
Boston	75.6	24.4
Bristol	38.0	62.0
Lambeth	21.4	78.6
Glasgow	33.4	66.6

slides.notes: CHART (bar) — identical text to a table slide; change the type and it draws. Several series means one press of Next lands a whole series; a single series means one press lands a category. Colours come from the validated palette, assigned in fixed order.

slides.name: 35 · Chart — line, for change over time

params.text: Chart — line, for change over time

slides.notes: CHART (line) — series names are drawn at the right-hand end rather than in a legend box, so the eye never has to travel. The right margin is measured from the longest name before drawing, and converging labels step apart. One press of Next draws a whole line.

slides.name: 36 · Chart — pie, for parts of one whole

params.text: Chart — pie, for parts of one whole

params.data:
Asia, 59
Africa, 18
Europe, 9
Americas, 13
Oceania, 1

slides.notes: CHART (pie) — only honest when the slices are parts of a single total and there are few of them. Two series will not work here. If you are comparing magnitudes rather than showing a composition, use the bar.

slides.name: 37 · Chart · ranking — what is the order?

params.text: Chart · ranking — what is the order?

params.data:
No local network, 62
Cost of travel, 48
No one to ask, 41
Timing of events, 23
Nothing nearby, 12

params.text: Source: Illustrative figures. Every chart carries a line like this one, and it prints under the drawing and into the student handout.

slides.notes:
RANKING — a sorted horizontal bar is the Financial Times’ own ranking chart, and the reason is that position on a common scale is the channel the eye reads most accurately. Sort it, or it is not a ranking chart.

This slide is also the one showing the SOURCE LINE. Where the numbers came from and what they are not — that is the thing a reader needs a week later with nobody there to explain it.

slides.name: 38 · Chart · part-to-whole — how does it divide up?

params.text: Chart · part-to-whole — how does it divide up?

params.data:
Year	Teaching	Research	Outreach
2023	52	31	17
2024	48	34	18
2025	44	35	21

slides.notes:
STACKED BAR — for composition over a few categories. It warns you if a series contains negatives, because those are silently left out of a total and the bar would lie.

Also in this family and drawn by the same picker: pie, donut, treemap and waffle.

slides.name: 39 · Chart · donut, and its cousins

params.data:
University, 44
Apprenticeship, 21
Bootcamp, 18
Self-taught, 17

slides.notes:
DONUT — a pie with the middle taken out, and the same paste. The hole buys you somewhere to put the total, which is the only real reason to prefer it.

Treemap and waffle are further on: the same data, the same question, two better answers to it.

slides.name: 40 · Chart · correlation — do two things move together?

params.text: Chart · correlation — do two things move together?

params.data:
Cohort	Hours on task	Mark
A	4	52
B	7	61
C	9	58
D	12	74
E	14	71
F	18	88
G	20	79

slides.notes:
SCATTER — a first column of words becomes each point’s label, and labels that would collide are moved and given a leader line. Read x, y with two columns; name, x, y with three.

The app says out loud what this chart cannot: readers will assume the relationship you draw is causal.

slides.name: 41 · Chart · distribution — what values occur, how often?

params.text: Chart · distribution — what values occur, how often?

slides.notes:
BOX PLOT — one row per group, then every value measured in it, so a column of marks pasted from a spreadsheet becomes this. Whiskers stop at the furthest real observation inside Tukey’s 1.5×IQR fence; anything past it is drawn as a point, which is why Group A has one at 88.

A histogram answers the same question for a single ungrouped column.

slides.name: 42 · Chart · flow — where does it go?

params.text: Chart · flow — where does it go?

params.data:
From	To	People
Applied	Interviewed	420
Applied	Rejected at sift	580
Interviewed	Offered	140
Interviewed	No offer	280
Offered	Joined	110
Offered	Declined	30

slides.notes: SANKEY — from, to, amount: a list of flows rather than a table of values. This is the honest alternative to a funnel, and the inspector points at it from there: a funnel shows what is left at each stage, a Sankey shows where the rest went. On this data that is 580 people rejected at sift who a funnel would simply not draw.

slides.name: 43 · Chart · magnitude — one icon is one unit

params.text: Chart · magnitude — one icon is one unit

params.data:
Stage	People
Applied	1000
Interviewed	420
Offered	140
Still there at year 3	62

slides.notes: PICTOGRAM — the ISOTYPE tradition: the icon repeats and never grows, so the count is read by counting rather than by judging an area. Set the glyph and how many each one stands for; the remainder is drawn as a clipped icon rather than a smaller one, because a smaller one would encode the value in area again.

slides.name: 44 · Chart · radar, and why to be careful

params.text: Chart · radar, and why to be careful

params.data:
Skill	Start of module	Now
Reading a chart	2	4
Choosing an idiom	1	3
Cleaning data	2	3
Writing the caption	1	4
Critique	2	4

slides.notes:
RADAR — defensible here and in few other places: the axes are the same kind of thing on the same nought-to-five scale, and the two shapes are the same learner at two times.

It repeats its own critique in the app, which is the point of drawing it at all: enclosed area grows as the SQUARE of the values, so a row twice as good encloses four times the shape — and reordering the spokes changes that area without changing the data.

slides.name: 45 · Chart · deviation — how far apart are two points?

params.text: Chart · deviation — how far apart are two points?

params.data:
Function	At entry (%)	At senior (%)
Engineering	8.9	3.1
Data	9.6	3.8
Product	7.2	2.4
Design	6.4	2.9

slides.notes:
DUMBBELL — two named series as two dots on one row, and the bar between them is the finding. The gap is printed on the row, because that is the number that gets quoted. Reach for it whenever you would otherwise draw two bars side by side and ask the room to subtract.

It carries a key, because which dot is which would otherwise live only in a tooltip — and a room looking at a projector has no tooltips.

slides.name: 46 · Chart · small multiples, on one stated scale

params.text: Chart · small multiples, on one stated scale

params.data:
Line	2021	2022	2023	2024
Central	18	22	26	31
Victoria	12	15	14	19
Northern	24	23	27	29
Bakerloo	9	11	13	12

params.text: Source: Illustrative. Every panel shares one scale, and the scale is written on the slide rather than left to be assumed.

slides.notes:
SMALL MULTIPLES — read transposed: each row is a panel and the columns are the axis inside it. The panels share a scale and the app says so on the drawing, because panels on their own scales are the most common way this chart misleads.

Past about a dozen panels it tells you a room cannot compare that many.

slides.name: 47 · Chart · against a target

params.data:
Measure	Actual	Target
Applications	1240	1000
Offers	860	800
Enrolled	510	600

slides.notes:
BULLET — a value against a reference: a target, a long-run average, or zero. The bar is the actual, the tick is the target, and nobody has to subtract.

The picker groups all twenty idioms by the question they answer rather than by what they look like, which is the Financial Times’ Visual Vocabulary rather than a gallery of shapes.

slides.name: 48 · Chart · area — a total, and what it is made of

params.text: Chart · area — a total, and what it is made of

slides.notes:
AREA — a line chart with the space underneath filled, stacked when there is more than one series. Read the top edge as the total and the bands as its composition.

The honest warning: only the bottom band sits on a flat baseline, so every band above it is harder to read on its own. If a single series is the story, draw it as a line.

slides.name: 49 · Chart · combo — two units on one slide

params.text: Chart · combo — two units on one slide

params.data:
Quarter	Events held	Average attendance
Q1	3	62
Q2	5	71
Q3	4	88
Q4	6	94

slides.notes:
COMBO — the first series draws as columns, every later one as markers on top. For a count and a rate together: the bars are how many, the markers are how well.

Use it when the two really are different units. Two series in the same unit belong on the same axis as two bars or two lines.

slides.name: 50 · Chart · histogram — the shape of one column

params.text: Chart · histogram — the shape of one column
Source: One cohort, one assessment. Bin edges are computed from the data, not chosen to flatter it.

slides.notes:
HISTOGRAM — paste one column of numbers and they are counted into bins for you. Where a box plot summarises a distribution in five numbers, this draws its actual shape, which is the only way a second peak shows up at all.

Bin width is a real editorial choice: too wide hides the shape, too narrow turns it into noise.

slides.name: 51 · Chart · treemap — parts of a whole, by area

params.text: Chart · treemap — parts of a whole, by area

params.data:
Spend	Share
Delivery	44
Venues	18
Bursaries	16
Research	12
Core costs	10

slides.notes:
TREEMAP — the same paste as a pie, drawn as nested rectangles. It holds more categories than a pie without collapsing into slivers, and rectangles are compared slightly better than angles.

Still area, though, and area is judged poorly. If the order is the message, draw the sorted bar.

slides.name: 52 · Chart · waffle — a hundred squares, so it can be counted

params.text: Chart · waffle — a hundred squares, so it can be counted

params.data:
Route in	Share
University	44
Apprenticeship	21
Bootcamp	18
Self-taught	17

slides.notes:
WAFFLE — a hundred squares, each one a percentage point. The reader counts rather than estimates, which is why this is the part-to-whole chart to choose when the exact figure matters as much as the split.

One square is never subdivided — five percent is five squares, and that is the whole point of the idiom.

slides.name: 53 · Chart · evidence matrix — ratings across conditions

params.text: Chart · evidence matrix — ratings across conditions

params.data:
Idiom	Spots the outlier	Shows the total	Holds 12 categories	Counts exactly
Sorted bar	Strong	Weak	Strong	Moderate
Stacked bar	Weak	Strong	Moderate	Weak
Pie	Weak	Strong	Weak	Weak
Box plot	Strong	Weak	Moderate	Weak
Scatter	Strong	Weak	Strong	Weak
Waffle	Weak	Strong	Weak	Strong
Sorted dumbbell	Moderate	Weak	Strong	Moderate

slides.notes:
EVIDENCE MATRIX — first row names the conditions, then one row per item with a rating in each cell. Words like Strong / Moderate / Weak are ranked once so the whole grid shares a single scale, which is what stops each column being read on its own.

For ordinal judgements — a systematic review, a shortlist against criteria, exactly this table of chart choices. Numbers in the cells belong in a table or a heatmap instead.

That is all twenty idioms the app draws. There are no maps, and the picker says so rather than leaving you to conclude it from an absence.

slides.name: 54 · Section · Pictures
slides.notes: Four ways a picture can carry a slide, and the caption and frame settings that apply across all of them.

slides.name: 55 · Full picture

params.text: Image — full bleed, caption over the picture
Northeastern University London · the City campus

slides.notes: IMAGE (full bleed) — the picture fills the slide and the caption sits on it under a gradient scrim, which reads over any image. Title is the caption line, subtitle the credit. Caption styles: scrim (default, safest), bar (solid), plain, none. Caption can sit top instead of bottom.

slides.name: 56 · Framed picture

params.text: Image — framed to a fixed ratio

slides.notes: IMAGE (framed) — the picture takes a shape of its own and the caption sits clear below it. Ratios: 16:9, 4:3, 3:2, 1:1, 4:5. Use a frame for anything with labels near the edge — a caption bar across the bottom of a chart covers its axis. Fit contain shows the whole image; cover crops it to fill.

args.caption: Image — framed to a fixed ratio

slides.name: 57 · Full picture

params.text: Every black bar is a death. The pump is in the middle of them.
John Snow, Broad Street, 1854 · lith. C. F. Cheffins

slides.notes:
A MOVING IMAGE — Design → Image motion → Slow zoom in. Twenty-four seconds, once, ending where it stops; it does not loop back and start again, because a picture that keeps restarting is a picture nobody finishes reading.

It zooms toward the Image focus point, which is why this one drifts into Broad Street rather than the middle of the plate. Set the focus first, then the motion.

Projector only. The editor holds it still so the preview is not re-animating every time you type, and a machine set to reduce motion gets the still picture — the slide still works, it simply stops moving.

The caption clears itself after ten seconds (Design → Caption clears itself). It names the plate while the room needs naming, then gets off the picture.

slides.name: 58 · The first pie chart anybody drew

params.text: The first pie chart anybody drew
The first pie chart anybody drew

Playfair had already invented the line chart and the bar chart twenty years earlier, in the Commercial and Political Atlas of 1786.

The circle was his answer to a different question: not how much, but how a single whole divides — here the Turkish Empire split across Europe, Asia and Africa.

He was ignored for most of a century. The chart was not.

slides.notes:
FLIP TO FACTS — put anything in the slide’s body and the picture gets a ⇄ in the corner. Press it and the same slide turns over: the facts on the back, the picture still there behind them, one more press and you are back.

The point is that you never leave the slide. The room is looking at the plate, you are asked where it came from, and answering it does not cost you the picture and a click forward and a click back. It is one slide with two faces rather than two slides in a row.

Works on the projector and in the editor. Nothing about it is a build step, so it does not consume a Next — which is exactly why it suits the question you did not plan for.

args.caption: The first pie chart anybody drew
args.facts:
Playfair had already invented the line chart and the bar chart twenty years earlier, in the Commercial and Political Atlas of 1786.
The circle was his answer to a different question: not how much, but how a single whole divides — here the Turkish Empire split across Europe, Asia and Africa.
He was ignored for most of a century. The chart was not.

slides.name: 59 · Split — picture on one side, points on the other

params.text: Split — picture on one side, points on the other

The picture takes one half, the points the other.
Image side can be left or right.
Use it when the picture is evidence for the points, not decoration beside them.

slides.notes: SPLIT — the compromise layout, and the one to be suspicious of. If the picture is not actually doing work, drop it and use a content slide. Set imageSide to left or right.

slides.name: 60 · Gallery — an image stack

params.text: Dataset I — a plain linear relationship
Dataset III — one outlier drags the line
Dataset IV — one point invents the slope

slides.notes: GALLERY — each press lays the next picture in front of the last, with its own caption and source, the earlier ones still showing at the edges. Up to eight layers. The effect is cumulative: the room sees the pile growing, which is what makes four near-identical scatterplots land. Every layer here has the same summary statistics.

figs.caption: Dataset I — a plain linear relationship
Dataset III — one outlier drags the line
Dataset IV — one point invents the slope

slides.name: 61 · Before and after
slides.notes: BEFORE / AFTER — drag the handle to wipe between two pictures. Only worth it when the two images are registered to each other — same framing, same scale — so the wipe compares like with like. A redesign, a map at two dates, a chart before and after a fix.

slides.name: 62 · Section · Things the room can touch
slides.notes: The interactive layouts. All of them work on the projector and on a learner phone in a live session.

slides.name: 63 · Explore — hotspots on one picture

params.text: Click to go through each numbered detail in order.
The tallest thing on the horizon, and the reason the eye lands here first.
Picked out in red while everything round it stays blue — colour doing the work of a label.
Every detail, back in its place.

slides.notes: EXPLORE — pin hotspots to a picture by percentage coordinates; each one zooms in and shows a title and a note. Use it to walk a room around a complicated image — a chart with several stories in it, a map, a screenshot of an interface.

spots.title: The Shard
spots.body: The tallest thing on the horizon, and the reason the eye lands here first.

spots.title: Tower Bridge
spots.body: Picked out in red while everything round it stays blue — colour doing the work of a label.

slides.name: 64 · Simulation — change an input, watch the output

params.text: Simulation — change an input, watch the output

slides.notes: SIMULATION — a slider bound to a model, drawn as a curve. Reach for it when the relationship is the lesson and a static chart would only show one point on it. Learners can drive their own copy from their phones.

slides.name: 65 · Links — the reading list
slides.notes: LINKS — text before the tab is the label, after it the URL. In a live session these become tappable on learner phones, which is the point: nobody copies a URL off a projector.

slides.name: 66 · Full picture

params.text: Same five numbers. Two different axes.

slides.notes:
VIDEO — a file beside the deck, or a YouTube or Vimeo link. Paste the share URL and it becomes an embed; paste a path and it becomes a real player with the projector’s own controls.

This one is set muted, looping and autoplaying, which is the combination that works on a wall: sound in a lecture theatre is a gamble, a loop means a latecomer still sees the whole thing, and autoplay saves you walking to the laptop. Autoplay is honoured on the projector and never in the editor — a preview that starts playing while you type is a preview you turn off.

Start and end are settable in seconds, so a forty-minute recording can contribute the ninety seconds you actually want without you editing the file. The poster is the frame it shows before it plays, and it is worth setting: without one the slide is a black rectangle until the first frame decodes.

An embedded clip draws a still in the editor rather than a dead frame, because loading the real player beside the inspector would start somebody’s video while they worked.

One thing worth copying: a video caption is a fixed band across the bottom of the frame, about 208px of white-on-gradient, and it clears the player controls rather than the content. So this clip was drawn with that band empty — the chart and its labels stop above it. If you are making the clip as well as the slide, leave the caption somewhere to sit.

slides.name: 67 · Video — what to check before the lecture

params.text: Video — what to check before the lecture
Plays with no network. This is the one to use when the room’s wifi is a rumour.
Becomes an embed on the no-cookie domain. Needs the network, and the site has to be reachable from the lecture theatre.
The wall combination. Sound only if you have tested the room’s sound.
Clip the ninety seconds you want out of a forty-minute recording, without editing the file.

slides.notes:
The clip on the previous slide is about 280 KB and travels with the deck, which is the whole argument for a file over a link: nothing to load, nothing to log in to, nothing that shows an advert first.

What it shows is the same five numbers twice — once on an axis that starts at zero, once on an axis that starts at 55. A bar encodes its value as a LENGTH, so cutting the baseline cuts away the part of the length that carries the value, and the differences that are left look several times larger than they are. It is the most common way a correct number tells a lie, and it is much easier to watch happen than to describe.

slides.name: 68 · Section · What the room does

params.text: Four ways a slide can ask, and one live check

slides.notes: Everything from here needs Host live and phones in the room. On the projector each of these draws its own control; on a learner phone the same control takes over the screen.

slides.name: 69 · Everyone in, in about twenty seconds

params.text: Everyone in, in about twenty seconds

Scan the code, or type the address and the four digits.
No app, no account, no name unless you ask for one.

slides.notes:
JOIN — the app builds this for you when you host a session, with the real room code in it. What you are looking at now is a sample, because this deck is not live.

Leave it on the wall while the room arrives. Latecomers join off the same code without stopping you.

LAB — In SlideForge this slide shows the live session’s join code and QR code; the lab has no live session, so it keeps the words.

slides.name: 70 · What it looks like in their hand

params.text: What it looks like in their hand

Their own first name at the top — and a question mark, a raised hand and a heart, so a room can interrupt without interrupting.
Under it, which slide the wall is on. That line is what stops “which one are we looking at?”
The heart saves this slide to their own copy, so revision is something they build while the lesson happens.
The poll itself takes the whole screen. There is nothing else on it to do.

slides.notes:
A REAL SCREENSHOT, not a drawing of one: this deck hosted, joined from a phone-sized browser, photographed mid-poll. The slide number on it is this deck with its games compiled out, which is why it counts past the ninety in the editor.

No app, no account, a first name only when the activity needs one — and somebody watching a follow-along screen is not in the register at all.

Regenerate all of these with tools/capture-phone.mjs whenever the learner screens change. A screenshot nobody can rebuild goes stale and then lies about the product.

slides.name: 71 · And when it is a check rather than a poll

params.text: And when it is a check rather than a poll

A to D, one tap, then “Locked in” — so they know the answer arrived.
Then, and only then: how sure are you? I’m sure, or just a guess.
A confident wrong answer is the most useful thing in the room. It is also the one a show of hands never tells you.
The same screen carries every engine — ranking, typing, estimating, the race, the boss.

slides.notes:
CONFIDENCE is optional on all twenty-three engines and off by default. Turn it on for the questions where being wrong-and-certain is the thing you need to catch.

The other captured screens — joining, the word cloud, the scale — are in assets/demo-phone if you want them in a deck of your own. They came out of the same run as these two.

slides.name: 72 · And afterwards, the same deck at their own pace

params.text: And afterwards, the same deck at their own pace

The read-only link opens on a phone as well as a laptop.
Arrows at the bottom, Full screen if they want it, and a count so they know how far there is to go.
No PIN, no room, no clock — and nothing they do here reaches your register.
Speaker notes are not in it. What they get is the slides.

slides.notes:
This is the first of the two shares, seen from the other end: the copy they page through themselves. Worth showing a client next to the live screens, because it answers the question every room asks at the end — “can we get the slides?” — without you emailing a 40 MB file.

The follow-along screen is the same address with one word added, and it is the one that moves when you move. Both are on the Share button, which asks which you want before it uploads anything.

slides.name: 73 · Poll — fixed options, counted live

params.text:
Add a feedback moment to any slide from the inspector.
The room answers on their phones; the bars fill in the rail beside the slide.
Use it to decide what to do next, not to score anybody.

slides.notes: POLL — the results are for you, in the room, now. Read the split out loud and change the next ten minutes because of it, or do not ask.

feedback.prompt: Which of these is the hardest to get right?

slides.name: 74 · Word cloud — one word each

params.text:
Short answers, repeats grow larger.
Best before you teach something, not after.

slides.notes: WORD CLOUD — keep it to a word each or the cloud becomes a paragraph nobody reads. A cloud of the room’s own words on the wall is the cheapest way to make a room feel present.

feedback.prompt: One word: what makes a chart honest?

slides.name: 75 · Brainstorm — longer contributions, newest first

params.text:
For sentences rather than single words.
Contributions arrive with names, so the room can be credited by name.
Read a few out. An unread brainstorm teaches the room not to bother next time.

slides.notes: BRAINSTORM — the widest of the four: no options, no scale, just what they want to say. It lists newest first so the wall keeps moving while people are still typing.

feedback.prompt: Name a chart you have seen this week that misled you — and say how.

slides.name: 76 · Scale — where do you stand?

params.text:
One position each, on an ordered run of points.
It reports the spread as well as the average — and the spread is usually the more interesting half.

slides.notes:
SCALE — a poll over points that have an order, so it earns a mean and a distribution rather than a set of independent bars. Name both ends of it, as this one does.

Read the spread out loud. A room split into two camps and a room that is uniformly unsure have the same average and need completely different next ten minutes.

feedback.prompt: How confident are you reading a box plot?

slides.name: 77 · A live check, mid-lesson

params.text: Read the question and choose an answer.

slides.notes:
A LIVE CHECK — built for you rather than chosen from the layout picker, which is why it is not in the bank above. Phones answer, you hold the reveal, and the explanation follows. Confidence is on here, so the room says how sure it is as well as what it thinks — a confident wrong answer being the most useful signal you can get.

The quiz, results, join and explain slides are made the same way, by the live session.

Check an idea; discuss the why.

slides.notes: The layouts above are shapes you fill in. An activity is the other direction: you pick the teaching move, and it writes the slides.

slides.name: 81 · The activity library

params.text: Filed under the eleven phases of a lesson — starter, activation, construction, mini, main, collaboration, mini-quiz, reflection, plenary.
Each one says what it costs
How long it takes, and what has to be in the room before you start.
Not a description of the activity. The actual slides, filled in, in your deck, ready to be rewritten.

slides.notes:
THE ACTIVITY LIBRARY — the Activities studio, or the library dialog from anywhere. Filter by phase and the list stops being fifty-four things and starts being the four that fit where you are.

Formats that are planned but not built are shown and disabled rather than hidden, so the list does not quietly imply the app can do less than it can — or more.

slides.name: 82 · Where an activity lands

params.text: Twenty-three write one finished slide, at the layout the activity needs.
Two write several, because the activity has stages.
Ten build a game and the slide that runs it.
Nine attach a prompt the room answers on their phones.

slides.notes:
The library tells you which of these an activity is before you pick it, because “adds a slide” and “runs for ten minutes with phones out” are different commitments.

Where the original teaching move did not fit an engine honestly, the entry says so and what it does instead. Card Sort wanted fifteen cards in student-chosen groups; Ranking allows eight in one line. So it writes the slide and leaves the cards on the table where they belong.

LAB — SlideForge shows 5 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: A live moment — Ten are run rather than drawn: a task, a timer, a break..

slides.name: 83 · Think-Pair-Share

params.text: On your own: which chart in this deck would you not have chosen? One line.
Swap with the person beside you and argue for the one you would keep.
Two pairs report out. I write the disagreement on the board.

slides.notes:
AN ACTIVITY SLIDE, as the library writes it — rail badge naming its phase, timings in the labels, the steps view so the three stages read as three stages.

The box underneath is a DRAFT ANSWER. Nineteen activities carry a worked answer in their teacher notes, and the library brings it across rather than leaving it where no room ever sees it. It arrives shut and marked: every one is written about somebody else’s subject, so showing it unread would put the wrong answer on the wall. Rewrite it and it becomes the card on the next slide.

slides.name: 84 · I do · We do · You do

params.text: I do · We do · You do
I build one chart from this table, saying every choice out loud.
We build the next one together — you tell me what to choose and why.
You build the third on your own. I say nothing.
Two of yours on the wall side by side, and we say why they differ.

slides.notes:
THE PANELS VIEW — four equal panels, and only at four: the view needs exactly that many, so three or five falls back to rows rather than drawing a gap. Gradual release is four moves, which is why it is the shape this activity uses.

Build on Next is on, so the room is not reading “you do” while you are still doing.

slides.name: 85 · Error analysis — find the faults

params.text: A pie with eleven slices, two of them 3%, no labels, ordered alphabetically.
Name each one, then say what it costs the reader.
One sentence: which idiom, and what its title would say.

slides.notes:
THE ANSWER CARD, rewritten and therefore live: the task is on the front and the worked answer is BEHIND it, not further down. Turning the card over is a deliberate act that happens when the time is up — so the room looks at the task for the whole of the activity instead of reading ahead.

The brief view sets the labels as headings, for an activity whose rows are instructions rather than vocabulary.

slides.name: 86 · A moment you run, not a slide you wrote

params.text: A moment you run, not a slide you wrote
Instructions over whatever is on screen, with a countdown if it needs one.
Thinking time on its own, so silence in the room is deliberate rather than awkward.
Five minutes, said out loud, so nobody has to ask.

slides.notes:
LIVE MOMENTS — started from the presenter desk or the controls on the wall, mid-slide, without leaving the show. The deadline is held by the host rather than each phone, so a learner joining late sees the same clock as everyone else and pausing pauses it for the room.

One refusal worth knowing: a moment will not start over a knowledge check that is still waiting to be revealed. That would cover the question with a countdown about something else.

slides.name: 87 · Section · Games
slides.notes: A game is its own document, joined to a slide. The three that follow are three different engines on the same subject, so what changes is the shape of the thinking rather than the topic.

slides.name: 88 · The game library

params.text: Multiple choice, true / false, ranking, typed answers, estimation, odd-one-out, definitions, memory pairs, heads-up, bingo, a horse race, a boss battle.
The same engines set up for a job: Beat the Clock, Spot the Error, Predict the Outcome, Fill in the Blanks, Concept Chain, Question Cube.
Between slides as their own board, or beside a slide as a quick check.

slides.notes:
THE GAME LIBRARY — the same dialog as the activities, and each card says how the room takes part before you pick it.

Every engine shares the same spine: phones answer, you hold the reveal, the explanation follows, and confidence is optional on all of them. What differs is what the wall does while the room is answering — which is most of whether a class leans in.

RANKING — one linear order, part marks for the items placed right, so a nearly-correct answer is not scored as a wrong one. Three to eight items; past eight the room is sorting rather than thinking.

Good for a process, a chronology, or a set of priorities. Bad for anything where two items genuinely tie, because the engine will insist on an order the subject does not have.

slides.name: 110 · Section · Running the room

params.text: Rehearse, present, host — and the two ways to share

slides.notes: Everything so far is what goes on the wall. This is what you are holding while it is up there.

slides.name: 111 · Four ways to run the same deck

params.text: Four ways to run the same deck
The whole lesson against a sample class — answers, scores and a room that is not there. Nothing counts.
The show on the wall. Arrow keys, or the controls that fade in when the mouse moves.
The same show with phones in it: a join code, answers coming back, the room in a rail beside the slide.
A second window for you alone — notes, what is next, who answered what, and the room. Press D.

slides.notes:
REHEARSE is the one most people never find, and the one worth finding: it fills the deck with a plausible class so you can see what a poll looks like with thirty answers in it before thirty people are watching you meet it.

Teacher Presenter wants a second screen. Without one, it is still the right window to have on a laptop while the projector shows the wall.

slides.name: 112 · The controls on the wall

params.data:
Control	Key	What it does
Back / forward	← →	One point at a time, on a slide that builds
Room view	S	Hidden, beside the slide, or full screen
Quick poll	V	Ask what you had not planned to ask
Freeze	Z	Hold the wall while you digress
Draw	I	Ink on the slide, or spotlight part of it
Blank	B	Black the projector · Shift+B the phones
Join code	J	The QR and PIN, full screen
Everything else	?	The full list of keys

slides.notes:
THE CONTROLS fade in when the mouse moves and fade out again, so a still wall is a slide rather than a slide with a toolbar on it. Everything here has a key, and the keys are the faster route.

Behind the ••• as well, each with its own key: the leaderboard (E), the room’s reactions on or off (T), who may speak (Shift+H), reset the scores (R), named answers in the presenter window (W), full screen (F), and the two pop-outs. FREEZE is the one to learn first — it is the difference between a digression and a scramble.

slides.name: 113 · Teacher Presenter — nine panels

params.data:
Panel	What it holds
Notes	Your notes for this slide, and the next slide beside them
Quick	A task with a countdown, a break, and five one-tap polls
Activities	The library, runnable mid-lesson without leaving the show
Pulse	Reactions and slide responses as they arrive
Answers	Who answered what — names, not only totals
Class	The register: who joined, who is still missing
Insights	Which questions the room found hard, and how sure it was
Tools	Name picker, timer, a scratch pad
Q&A	Questions from phones, with a badge when one is waiting

slides.notes:
This window is private. The projector never shows it, which is why the notes you are reading live here rather than on the slide.

It opens as a real pop-out — drag it to a second screen, or keep it on the laptop while the wall runs the show. Press D from the show, or the button in the bar before you start.

slides.name: 114 · Two ways to share, and they are not the same thing

params.text: Two ways to share, and they are not the same thing
No — works whether or not you are presenting
Yes — Host live first, or the option is greyed out with the reason on it
They do: their pace, their order, their own time
You do: it moves when you move, including through a build, and cannot run ahead
Revision afterwards, and the person who missed the lesson
A second projector, an overflow room, a desktop at the back of the hall
None. The address is the whole secret
None either — and nobody watching appears in your register or your reports

slides.notes:
SHARE asks which of these you want before it uploads anything, because they come out of one copy and answer completely different questions. Each gets its own QR code and its own address.

What both mean: a copy on this server at an address nobody can guess, unlisted and read-only — but a link that escapes is a lesson that escaped. Games are not carried across; the slides are. You get a key that withdraws it, and it is the only way to.

slides.name: 115 · Section · Two settings that apply everywhere

params.text: Build on Next, and the theme

slides.notes: Worth knowing before you start copying slides out of this deck.

slides.name: 116 · What carries across every layout

params.text: Reveal a slide piece by piece rather than all at once. Per slide, not per deck.
Hide keeps the next point secret. Dim leaves earlier points on screen at 38%.
Set on the deck. Every layout here redraws in any of the themes.
What you are reading now. Visible on the presenter desk, never on the projector.

slides.notes:
Be strategic with dim. It suits a list where the earlier points are still doing work — a framework, a set of criteria. It is wrong where the next point is a reveal, or where the slide is already busy.

LAB — SlideForge shows 5 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Logo — Set on the deck, drawn top right. Keep a slide title under about 40 characters so it cannot run under it..

slides.name: 117 · Using this bank

params.text:
Page through it once to see what exists.
Found a shape you want? Copy the slide (⌘C) and paste it into your own deck (⌘V), then replace the content.
Layouts are app-wide — every one of these is already in the layout picker of every deck you open.
This deck is a reference copy. Edit it freely; rebuild it from the lesson picker whenever you want a clean one.
Not chosen from the picker: quiz, results and explain. Those are built by the live session.

slides.notes: Close. Rebuilding this lesson gives a fresh copy, so nothing here is precious. Every layout the picker offers is in this deck, video included — it plays a clip that ships with the deck rather than pointing at a URL that might not answer. Three slide types never appear in the picker at all: quiz and results are built by the live session, and explain is the card that shows the correct answer after a check — which is also why the student handout leaves it out.
